Assess where predictions extrapolate beyond the data

Source: R/extrapolation.R
assess_extrapolation.Rd

Computes, for each prediction location, indicators of whether a prediction from a fitted geostatistical model relies on extrapolation, either in space (where the data say little about the spatial effect) or in the covariates (outside the conditions observed in the data).

Usage

assess_extrapolation(
  object,
  newdata,
  spatial_threshold = NULL,
  sampling_noise = TRUE
)

# S3 method for class 'RiskMap_extrapolation'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

object

A fitted RiskMap model.

newdata

An sf object of prediction points with the covariates used by the model, typically a grid from create_grid().

spatial_threshold

Threshold of the share of the spatial variance left unexplained above which a location is classed as spatial extrapolation. NULL (the default) uses the 95th percentile of the shares left at the sampled locations when their own data are left out (see Details). A number strictly between 0 and 1 gives a fixed threshold.

sampling_noise

Whether the share of the spatial variance left unexplained includes the sampling noise of the outcomes (the default). With FALSE, it depends only on where the data were collected and on the nugget, as if the spatial effect had been observed without noise at every sampled location.

x

A RiskMap_extrapolation object, whose print() method counts the locations in each class and states the thresholds of the classes, returning x invisibly.

...

Not used, and an error if given, so that a misspelt argument is not ignored. A subset that lost the classes or the threshold prints as an sf object, and the arguments go to its print method.

Value

An sf object of class RiskMap_extrapolation with the rows and geometry of newdata and the columns

covariates_outside

Number of covariates outside their observed range.

covariate_novelty

Largest distance outside an observed range, as a share of that range (0 when all are within range).

most_novel_covariate

Name of the design-matrix column with the largest distance outside its range, or NA.

covariate_leverage

Leverage relative to its maximum over the data.

spatial_unexplained

Share of the spatial variance left unexplained by the data, \(v(x)\).

extrapolation

Factor with levels "Supported", "Spatial", "Covariate" and "Spatial and covariate".

Rows with missing covariates have missing indicators. The attribute spatial_threshold holds the threshold used, and covariate_ranges the range of each covariate in the data. Map the result with plot.RiskMap_extrapolation().

Details

Covariates are assessed on the model's scale, that is, as the columns of the fixed-effect design matrix. A model with log(elevation) is therefore assessed on log elevation, and a spline in age through each of its basis columns. For each column, the distance outside the range observed in the data is expressed as a share of that range.

The leverage \(h(x) = d(x)^\top (D^\top D)^{-1} d(x)\), where \(D\) is the fitted design matrix, is reported relative to its maximum over the data. Values above 1 indicate a combination of covariates that is more unusual than any in the data, even when each covariate is within its range.

The share of the spatial variance left unexplained is $$v(x) = 1 - \rho(x)^\top (R + \sigma^{-2} W)^{-1} \rho(x),$$ where \(\rho(x)\) holds the estimated correlations between \(x\) and the sampled locations, \(R\) their correlation matrix, \(\sigma^2\) the spatial variance, and \(W\) a diagonal matrix with \(w_j = \tau^2 + c_j\), the nugget variance plus the sampling variance of the linear predictor at the sampled location \(j\). For a Gaussian model, \(c_j\) is the measurement-error variance divided by the number of records at the location, and \(v(x)\) is \(\mathrm{Var}[S(x) \mid y] / \sigma^2\) at the estimated parameters. For binomial, Poisson and negative binomial models, \(c_j\) is the inverse of the information \(-\partial^2 \log f(y \mid \eta) / \partial \eta^2\) of the records at the location, summed over them and evaluated at the conditional mode of the spatial effect given the data at the estimated parameters, so that \(v(x)\) is the Laplace approximation of \(\mathrm{Var}[S(x) \mid y] / \sigma^2\). With sampling_noise = FALSE, \(c_j = 0\).

\(v(x)\) is close to 0 where the data determine the spatial effect and close to 1 where they carry no information about it. Unlike the distance to the nearest sampled location, it accounts for the estimated scale of spatial correlation, for clustering of the sampled locations and for how much the data at each location say about the spatial effect, which is little where few individuals were sampled or where a prevalence is close to 0 or 1. The variances of re() terms are not included in \(W\), so for models with re() terms \(v(x)\) is lower than the share they leave.

A location is classed as covariate extrapolation when any covariate lies outside its observed range or its relative leverage exceeds 1, and as spatial extrapolation when \(v(x)\) exceeds the threshold. By default the threshold is the 95th percentile over the sampled locations \(s_j\) of $$v_{-j} = \mathrm{Var}[S(s_j) \mid y_{-j}] / \sigma^2 = 1 / [(R + \sigma^{-2} W)^{-1}]_{jj} - w_j / \sigma^2,$$ the share left at \(s_j\) by the data of the other locations. Leave-one-out cross-validation predicts at each sampled location from the others, so the \(v_{-j}\) are the amounts of spatial information under which predictions can be checked against held-out data, and a location above their 95th percentile has less than nearly all of them. A percentile rather than the largest value keeps a single remote sampled location from setting the threshold. The percentile is 1 only when the data of the other locations say nothing about the spatial effect at more than 5% of the sampled locations, as when the locations share almost no spatial correlation. No location can then be classed as spatial extrapolation, so assess_extrapolation() warns, and a fixed spatial_threshold is more informative. The two classes are kept separate because they call for different responses: more sampling where data are sparse, and caution about the form of the covariate effects outside the observed conditions.

See also

plot.RiskMap_extrapolation(), predict.RiskMap()

Examples

data(italy_sim)
example_data <- italy_sim[1:150, ]
fit <- glgpm(y ~ log(pop_dens) + gp(), data = example_data,
             family = "gaussian", messages = FALSE)
extrapolation <- assess_extrapolation(fit, italy_sim[151:200, ])
extrapolation
#> ── Extrapolation ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Indicators at 50 locations.
#> 
#> Supported              30
#> Spatial                20
#> Covariate               0
#> Spatial and covariate   0
#> 
#> ℹ Spatial: more than 82.7% of the spatial variance left unexplained, the 95th
#>   percentile of the shares at the sampled locations when their own data are
#>   left out.
#> ℹ Covariate: a covariate outside its range in the data, or a leverage above its
#>   largest value there.
#> ℹ `plot(x)` maps the classes, and `indicator = "spatial_unexplained"` the
#>   share.
table(extrapolation$extrapolation)
#> 
#>             Supported               Spatial             Covariate 
#>                    30                    20                     0 
#> Spatial and covariate 
#>                     0
